reader.title: Littleton dance hall shooting
bases: A group of drunken white men, refused dances by Black women, returned armed and fired on a Black dance hall, killing one man and wounding several (A1).
The only report is an Iowa editorial's quotation of an unseen telegram in an Atlanta paper (A1); no other white or Black paper carrying it was found.

summary.text: The Littleton dance hall shooting was an attack on a Black dance in a town called Littleton, on a Saturday night shortly before mid-October 1903, in which a group of drunken white men fired on the dancers after Black women refused to dance with them.
James Matthews was killed and several others were seriously wounded.

The shooting is known from a short telegram in an Atlanta paper, which an Iowa editor reprinted to contrast the muted response with what the editor said would follow an attack by Black men on white dancers.
According to the telegram, the white men passed "a negro hall where the blacks were dancing" and asked that the Black women dance with them.
When the women refused, the group left but came back later "with guns and pistols" and repeated the request, which was again refused.
The men then opened fire on the people in the hall, killing James Matthews, described as "one of the negroes," and seriously wounding several others.
The telegram ended with the line "The coroner is investigating."
None of the attackers was named, and no report of an inquest verdict, arrests or a trial appears in the coverage.

The only surviving account is in the "Topics of the Times" editorial column of the Evening Times-Republican of Marshalltown, Iowa, on October 16, 1903, which quoted what it called "an obscure ten-line telegram in an Atlanta paper."
The column neither named the state in which Littleton lay nor gave the date of the original dispatch.
The Iowa editor used the item to argue a double standard: had "drunken black men" attacked a white dancing party, the editor wrote, the newspapers of every state could not have held the headlines.
Instead of a coroner's investigation, the column said, every Black man, for which it used a slur in quotation marks, "would have been burned at the stake."
No other white paper reprinting the telegram, and no Black newspaper account of the shooting, was found.

sources.note: 'Topics of the Times' editorial quoting a ten-line telegram from an Atlanta paper on the Littleton shooting, then contrasting it with the reaction had Black men attacked a white dance.
quotes: An obscure ten-line telegram in an Atlanta paper tells the following story
At Littleton Saturday night a batch of drunken white men passed a negro hall where the blacks were dancing.
The drunken gang then retired, but returned later with guns and pistols and renewed their request, which was again refused.
James Matthews, one of the negroes, was killed and several were seriously wounded. The coroner is investigating.
Supposing drunken black men had thus attacked a dancing party of whites. The newspapers of every state in the union would have been unable to accommodate the headlines.
